item.title: Profile-guided LLVM Optimization
item.description:
Modern processors are incredibly fast, but memory latency remains a major bottleneck for performance. Compiler optimizations that restructure code to improve cache behavior and instruction efficiency can have a significant impact. In this project, I explored and implemented two profile-guided optimizations within the LLVM compiler framework.

Both techniques use dynamic profiling information to make more informed decisions during compilation—targeting performance gains that go beyond traditional static analysis.

Frequent Path Loop-Invariant Code Motion (FPLICM)

Traditional LICM hoists loop-invariant instructions outside of loops to avoid redundant computations. However, it must guarantee correctness across all paths within a loop, often leaving optimization opportunities untapped.

FPLICM builds on this by identifying instructions that are invariant along the most frequent execution path, even if they vary on rare paths. These “almost invariant” instructions are speculatively hoisted based on profiling data. If the program later takes an infrequent path, a lightweight repair mechanism ensures correctness by re-executing the hoisted code.

This speculative approach increases optimization aggressiveness while preserving correctness, leveraging the observation that most programs exhibit strong execution locality in loops.

Profile-Guided Software Prefetching

To address cache miss latency, I developed a profile-guided software prefetching pass. Unlike static approaches that require manually tuning prefetch distances, this optimization utilizes profile information from Intel’s Last Branch Record (LBR) to determine the best prefetch distance and prefetch injection site.

In testing, this technique improved performance effectively, especially for loops with indirect memory accesses—cases where hardware prefetchers typically fall short.

item.title: SQL Query Superoptimization
item.description:
SQL queries, if written poorly, are slow on large databases, even using state-of-the-art query optimizers.

In this project, we aim to leverage program synthesis, an area at the intersection of programming systems and artificial intelligence, to develop a SQL synthesizer that optimizes slow queries. With our unique benchmark collected from Leetcode and testing procedure incorporating fake data generation with Faker and runtime analysis with PostgreSQL cost model, we developed a solid understanding of what caused the queries to be slow, as well as how to rewrite/optimize them.

The current infrastructure includes transformation rules and a verifier. For queries rewriting, we have rule-based transformation, where a queries is evaluated on a set of rewrite rules, and if the queries match conditions for any rules, the query will undergo transformation at the abstract syntax tree (AST) level, resulting in optimized queries. However, there are conditions where no pattern could be found for the queries, we use a search-based technique to restructure part of the query to achieve optimization, based on our understanding of what makes a query have a shorter runtime.

item.title: Optimal Control of Inkjet Printing
item.description:
Machine learning embodies great potential in many interdisciplinary applications. In this project, we aim to find the optimal printing parameter of inkjet printers using machine learning methods.

We developed sampling methods for the experimental design, and our collaborator at Boise State University produced product lines based on our parameters combination and took microscope images of those lines.

We then developed image processing algorithms to calculate features of the printed lines. Multiple models were trained and compared and we eventually used neural networks as surrogate models for printing quality prediction.

item.title: Racial Disparity in SpO2
item.description:
Prior study at Michigan Medicine shows that the oxygen saturation (SpO2) measurement produced by pulse oximeters is biased toward people of color.

In this project at the Michigan Center for Integrative Research in Critical Care, we assessed the quality of SpO2 derived from patient’s bedside monitors and compared them with the gold standard arterial blood gas (ABG) results to look for potential bias.

SpO2 values that are potentially generated from noisy photoplethysmography (PPG) signals may be inaccurate. In particular, we augmented the PhysioNet Cardiovascular Signal Toolbox to assess the quality of each beat, and therefore determine how trustworthy a particular SpO2 value is. We also designed post-processing pipelines to enforce stricter requirements for a beat to be considered acceptable.

item.title: Lecture Capture Improvement
item.description:
The Lecture Capture System at CAEN captures high-quality images from the whiteboards in the classrooms. However, image quality can be poor in certain lighting conditions, and images often take up a lot of space and time to process.

Working as an Instructional Technology Developer at CAEN, I developed an algorithm to enhance the appearance of pen strokes against the noisy, unevenly lit background after completing a literature review on whiteboard enhancement, improving the legibility of whiteboards in even the worst lighting conditions. For the issue of unnecessary saving and processing of images, I developed a method to detect unchanged image frames based on differences in Normalized Cross-Correlation, thereby eliminating the need to process those images.
